questions.problem: Find the directional derivative of the function $f(x,y)=6{x}^{2}+2y$ at the point $(0,1)$ in the direction of the vector $v=3i+5j.$
questions.worked_solution:
The directional derivative ${f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)$ of a function $f(x,y)$ at the point $(a,b)$ in the direction of the vector $v$ is given by

$$
{f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)=∇f(a,b)\cdot u
$$

where $u$ is a unit vector in the direction of $v.$

First, we find the unit vector $u$ in the direction of $v:$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖v‖ & =\sqrt{{3}^{2}+{5}^{2}}=\sqrt{34} \\ u & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{34}}(3i+5j)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the gradient $∇f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $(0,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(6{x}^{2}+2y)\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(6{x}^{2}+2y)\text{ }j \\  & =12x\,i+2\,j \\ ∇\,f(0,1) & =(12\cdot 0)\,i+2\,j \\  & =2j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the directional derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{u}^{′}(0,1) & =∇\,f(0,1)\cdot u \\  & =2j\cdot (\frac{3}{\sqrt{34}}i+\frac{5}{\sqrt{34}}j) \\  & =\frac{0\cdot 3+2\cdot 5}{\sqrt{34}} \\  & =\frac{10\sqrt{34}}{34}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the directional derivative of the function $f(x,y)=x{e}^{y}+{x}^{2}y$ at the point $A(1,0)$ in the direction towards the point $B(0,1).$
questions.worked_solution:
The directional derivative ${f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)$ of a function $f(x,y)$ at the point $(a,b)$ in the direction of the vector $v$ is given by

$$
{f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)=∇f(a,b)\cdot u
$$

where $u$ is a unit vector in the direction of $v.$

First, we find the direction vector and the corresponding unit vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB} & =⟨0,1⟩-⟨1,0⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,1⟩ \\ u & =\frac{\overset{\to }{AB}}{‖\overset{\to }{AB}‖} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}}}⟨-1,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨-1,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the gradient $∇f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $A(1,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{e}^{y}+{x}^{2}y),\,\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{e}^{y}+{x}^{2}y)⟩ \\  & =⟨{e}^{y}+2xy,\,x{e}^{y}+{x}^{2}⟩ \\ ∇\,f(1,0) & =⟨{e}^{0}+2\cdot 1\cdot 0,\,1\cdot {e}^{0}+{1}^{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the directional derivative is:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{u}^{′}(1,0) & =∇f(1,0)\cdot u \\  & =⟨1,\,2⟩\cdot ⟨-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}},\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟩ \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the directional derivative of the function $f(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})$ at the point $(0,-1)$ in the direction of the vector $v=3\,i+4\,j.$
questions.worked_solution:
The directional derivative ${f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)$ of a function $f(x,y)$ at the point $(a,b)$ in the direction of the vector $v$ is given by

$$
{f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)=∇f(a,b)\cdot u
$$

where $u$ is a unit vector in the direction of $v.$

First, we find the unit vector $u$ in the direction of $v:$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖v‖ & =\sqrt{{3}^{2}+{4}^{2}}=5 \\ u & =\frac{1}{5}(3\,i+4\,j)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the gradient $∇f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $(0,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}))\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}))\text{ }j \\  & =\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,i+\frac{2y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}j \\ ∇\,f(0,-1) & =\frac{2(0)}{{0}^{2}+(-1)^{2}}\,i+\frac{2(-1)}{{0}^{2}+(-1)^{2}}\,j \\  & =-2\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the directional derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{u}^{′}(0,-1) & =∇\,f(0,-1)\cdot u \\  & =-2\,j\cdot \frac{1}{5}(3\,i+4\,j) \\  & =-\frac{2(4)}{5} \\  & =-\frac{8}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the directional derivative of the function $f(x,y)=xy$ at the point $(2,1)$ in the direction of the vector $v=\sqrt{3}\,i+j.$
questions.worked_solution:
The directional derivative ${f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)$ of a function $f(x,y)$ at the point $(a,b)$ in the direction of the vector $v$ is given by

$$
{f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)=∇f(a,b)\cdot u
$$

where $u$ is a unit vector in the direction of $v.$

First, we find the unit vector $u$ in the direction of $v:$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖v‖ & =\sqrt{(\sqrt{3})^{2}+{1}^{2}}=2 \\ u & =\frac{1}{2}(\sqrt{3}\,i+j)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the gradient $∇f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $(2,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(xy)\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(xy)\text{ }j \\  & =y\,i+x\,j \\ ∇\,f(2,1) & =i+2\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the directional derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{u}^{′}(2,1) & =∇\,f(2,1)\cdot u \\  & =(i+2\,j)\cdot \frac{1}{2}(\sqrt{3}\,i+j) \\  & =\frac{1(\sqrt{3})+2(1)}{2} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}+2}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the directional derivative of the function $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-xy$ at the point $(1,1)$ in the direction of the vector $v=i-j.$
questions.worked_solution:
The directional derivative ${f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)$ of a function $f(x,y)$ at the point $(a,b)$ in the direction of the vector $v$ is given by

$$
{f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)=∇f(a,b)\cdot u
$$

where $u$ is a unit vector in the direction of $v.$

First, we find the unit vector $u$ in the direction of $v:$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖v‖ & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+(-1)^{2}}=\sqrt{2} \\ u & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(i-j)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the gradient $∇f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $(1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-xy)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-xy)j \\  & =(2x-y)\,i+(2y-x)\,j \\ ∇\,f(1,1) & =(2(1)-1)\,i+(2(1)-1)\,j \\  & =i+j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the directional derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{u}^{′}(1,1) & =∇\,f(1,1)\cdot u \\  & =(i+j)\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(i-j) \\  & =\frac{1(1)+1(-1)}{\sqrt{2}} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Given the function $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x+y)+3{z}^{2}x$, in what direction does the function increase most rapidly at the point $(1,0,1)?$
questions.worked_solution:
At a given point, a function $f(x,y,z)$ increases most rapidly in the direction of its gradient at that point.

So, we compute $∇f(x,y,z)$ and evaluate it at the point $(1,0,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x+y)+3{z}^{2}x),\,\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x+y)+3{z}^{2}x),\,\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x+y)+3{z}^{2}x)⟩ \\  & =⟨\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x+y)+3{z}^{2},\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x+y),\,6xz⟩ \\ ∇f(1,0,1) & =⟨\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi \cdot 1+0)+3\cdot {1}^{2},\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi \cdot 1+0),\,6\cdot 1\cdot 1⟩ \\  & =⟨\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )+3,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi ),\,6⟩ \\  & =⟨-\pi +3,\,-1,\,6⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the function increases most rapidly in the direction of $⟨-\pi +3,\,-1,\,6⟩.$

questions.problem: Consider the function $f(x,y)=(x+y)\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y).$ What is the rate of change of $f(x,y)$ at the point $(2,-1)$ in the direction in which the function decreases most rapidly?
questions.worked_solution:
At a given point, a function $f(x,y)$ decreases most rapidly in the opposite direction of its gradient at that point.

In our case, we compute $-∇f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $(2,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}-∇\,f(x,y) & =-\frac{∂}{∂x}((x+y)\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y))\text{ }i-\frac{∂}{∂y}((x+y)\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y))\text{ }j \\  & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)+1)\text{ }i+(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)+1)\text{ }j \\ -∇\,f(2,-1) & =-(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2-1)+1)i-(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2-1)+1)j \\  & =-i-j\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the rate of change of $f(x,y)$ at the point $(2,-1)$ in the direction of $-∇f(2,-1)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}‖-∇\,f(2,-1)‖ & =‖-i-j‖ \\  & =\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+(-1)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Consider the function $g(x,y)=\frac{x}{y}+\frac{y}{x}.$ What is the rate of change of $g(x,y)$ at the point $(-1,1)$ in the direction of the vector $v=⟨1,-\sqrt{2}⟩?$
questions.worked_solution:
The rate of change of $g(x,y)$ at the point $(-1,1)$ in the direction of $v$ is equal to the directional derivative ${g}_{u}^{′}(-1,1).$ 

First, we find the unit vector $u$ in the direction of $v:$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖v‖ & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+(-\sqrt{2})^{2}}=\sqrt{3} \\ u & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨1,-\sqrt{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find the gradient $∇g(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $(-1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇g(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{x}{y}+\frac{y}{x}),\,\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{x}{y}+\frac{y}{x})⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{y}-\frac{y}{{x}^{2}},\,\frac{1}{x}-\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}⟩ \\ ∇g(-1,1) & =⟨\frac{1}{1}-\frac{1}{(-1)^{2}},\frac{1}{(-1)}-\frac{(-1)}{{1}^{2}}⟩ \\  & =⟨0,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the directional derivative ${g}_{u}^{′}(-1,1)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}_{u}^{′}(-1,1) & =∇g(-1,1)\cdot u \\  & =⟨0,0⟩\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨1,-\sqrt{2}⟩ \\  & =\frac{0(1)+0(-\sqrt{2})}{\sqrt{3}} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The rate of change of $g(x,y)$ at the point $(\frac{\pi }{4},\frac{\pi }{4})$ in the direction of $v$ is equal to the directional derivative ${g}_{u}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4},\frac{\pi }{4}).$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖v‖ & =\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}}=\sqrt{2} \\ u & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨-1,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find the gradient $∇\,g(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $(\frac{\pi }{4},\frac{\pi }{4}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,g(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x\operatorname{tan}⁡y-2y\operatorname{tan}⁡x),\,\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x\operatorname{tan}⁡y-2y\operatorname{tan}⁡x)⟩ \\  & =⟨2\operatorname{tan}⁡y-2y{sec}^{2}⁡x,\,2x{sec}^{2}⁡y-2\operatorname{tan}⁡x⟩ \\ ∇\,g(\frac{\pi }{4},\frac{\pi }{4}) & =⟨2\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})-2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4}\cdot {sec}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}),\,2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4}\cdot {sec}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})-2\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})⟩ \\  & =⟨2\cdot 1-\frac{\pi }{2}\cdot 2,\frac{\pi }{2}\cdot 2-2\cdot 1⟩ \\  & =⟨2-\pi ,\,\pi -2⟩\end{aligned}

Finally, the directional derivative ${g}_{u}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4},\frac{\pi }{4})$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}_{u}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4},\frac{\pi }{4}) & =∇\,g(\frac{\pi }{4},\frac{\pi }{4})\cdot u \\  & =⟨2-\pi ,\pi -2⟩\cdot ⟨-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}},\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟩ \\  & =\frac{(2-\pi )\cdot (-1)+(\pi -2)\cdot 1}{\sqrt{2}} \\  & =\frac{2\pi -4}{\sqrt{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{2}(\pi -2).\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Find the directional derivative of the function $g(x, y) =3x^2+4xy$ at the point $A(0,1)$ in the direction towards the point $B(1,4).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The directional derivative $g'_{\mathbf u}(a,b)$ of a function $g(x,y)$ at the point $(a,b)$ in the direction of the vector $\mathbf v$ is given by

$$
g'_{\mathbf u}(a,b) = \nabla g(a,b)\cdot\mathbf u
$$

where $\mathbf u$ is a unit vector in the direction of $\mathbf v.$

First, we find the direction vector and the corresponding unit vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB} & =⟨1,4⟩-⟨0,1⟩ \\  & =⟨1,3⟩ \\ u & =\frac{\overset{\to }{AB}}{‖\overset{\to }{AB}‖} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{3}^{2}}}⟨1,3⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}⟨1,3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the gradient $\nabla g(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $A(0,1)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇g(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(3{x}^{2}+4xy),\frac{∂}{∂y}(3{x}^{2}+4xy)⟩ \\  & =⟨6x+4y,\,4x⟩ \\ ∇g(0,1) & =⟨6\cdot 0+4\cdot 1,\,4\cdot 0⟩ \\  & =⟨4,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the directional derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}_{u}^{′}(0,1) & =∇g(0,1)\cdot u \\  & =⟨4,0⟩\cdot ⟨\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}},\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}⟩ \\  & =\frac{4}{\sqrt{10}} \\  & =\frac{4\sqrt{10}}{10} \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{10}}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Direction of Maximum Increase or Maximum Decrease of a Function
canonical_examples.problem: In what direction does the function $f (x, y) = \ln (x^2y)$ decrease most rapidly at the point $(2, 1)?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
At a given point, a function $f(x,y)$ decreases most rapidly in the direction opposite to that of its gradient.

So, we compute $-\nabla f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $(2,1)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}-∇f(x,y) & =-\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}y))\text{ }i-\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}y))\text{ }j \\  & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}y}\cdot 2xy\text{ }i-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}y}\cdot {x}^{2}j \\  & =-\frac{2}{x}\text{ }i-\frac{1}{y}\text{ }j \\ -∇f(2,1) & =-\frac{2}{2}\text{ }i-\frac{1}{1}\text{ }j \\  & =-i-j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the function decreases most rapidly in the direction of $- \, \mathbf i - \mathbf j.$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Rate of Change of a Function in a Given Direction
canonical_examples.problem: Consider the function $g (x, y) = \ln \left(\sqrt {xy^3}\right).$ What is the rate of change of $g$ at the point $\left(\dfrac 12, \dfrac 32 \right)$ in the direction in which the function increases most rapidly?
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
At a given point, a function $g(x,y)$ increases most rapidly in the direction of its gradient at that point.

In our case, we compute $\nabla g(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $\left(\dfrac 12, \dfrac 32 \right)\!\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇g(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt{x{y}^{3}})),\,\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt{x{y}^{3}}))⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{\sqrt{x{y}^{3}}}\cdot \frac{{y}^{3}}{2\sqrt{x{y}^{3}}},\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{x{y}^{3}}}\cdot \frac{3x{y}^{2}}{2\sqrt{x{y}^{3}}}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{2x},\,\frac{3}{2y}⟩ \\ ∇g(\frac{1}{2},\frac{3}{2}) & =⟨\frac{1}{2\cdot (\frac{1}{2})},\frac{3}{2\cdot (\frac{3}{2})}⟩ \\  & =⟨1,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the rate of change of $g(x,y)$ at the point $\left(\dfrac 12, \dfrac 32 \right)$ in the direction of $\nabla g\left(\dfrac 12, \dfrac 32 \right)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}‖∇g(\frac{1}{2},\frac{3}{2})‖ & =‖⟨1,1⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$
